title: ✍️ Writer's Room Coach
description: You're in a real writer's room. Each round, you'll write a short piece and get coaching feedback on the four pillars of strong writing: clarity, structure, voice, and revision. Build a real writing portfolio — from a 3-line story to a full personal essay.
subject: english
how_to_play: Each round you'll receive a short writing prompt.
Write your response in the textbox — short or long, your call.
Then choose how you'd refine it (the choices teach craft).
Each choice scores against the four pillars: clarity, structure, voice, revision.
By the end, you'll have a portfolio of 5-6 pieces and a writer's profile.
learning_objectives: Distinguish vague writing from specific writing.
Find your VOICE — the writing only you can produce.
Practice revision as part of the craft, not failure.
cultural_context: Personal narrative writing is core to NEP 2020 language curriculum and life-skill communication.

tick_rules: Each round = one piece in your portfolio

rounds.situation: Your prompt: write 2-3 lines about your favourite place. Most writers start vague. The skill is being SPECIFIC. The first sentence below is vague. Pick how YOU'd revise it.
rounds.coaching_moment: Vague writing is the #1 sign of an undeveloped writer. Concrete details make readers SEE.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why does 'specific' often feel harder than 'general'?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon writer at messy desk with notebook, friendly fox mascot Mento pointing at sentence on page, warm cozy room, kid-friendly

input_field.label: Quick: write 2 lines about your favourite place. (Optional but encouraged.)

rounds.vague_example: I really like my favourite place. It is so nice and cozy.

choices.label: A. 'I like the cozy, comfortable place where I always feel happy.'
choices.outcome_text: Stacking adjectives ('cozy', 'comfortable', 'happy') doesn't add specificity — it adds noise.

choices.label: B. 'My grandmother's terrace at 4pm, when the parrots come for the chillis drying on the ledge.'
choices.outcome_text: Beautiful. We can see the parrots, smell the chillis, feel the time of day. THAT is good writing.

choices.label: C. 'A quiet room with books and tea where I think.'
choices.outcome_text: OK, but every writer's described this. What's YOURS that nobody else has?

choices.label: D. 'It's amazing and I love it so much, you wouldn't believe how special it is.'
choices.outcome_text: Telling, not showing. The reader has no image. Try again with a *thing* you can see.

rounds.situation: Your prompt: a story about a misunderstanding. Of these openings, which is the strongest HOOK?
rounds.coaching_moment: Readers decide in 5-10 seconds. Your first sentence has to *grab*.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why does a strong hook usually involve specificity, surprise, or tension?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon hand holding fishing rod with question marks on hook, books and pages flying around, educational illustration, warm colors

input_field.label: Try writing your own hook for a story about a misunderstanding (1 sentence).

choices.label: A. 'There was once a boy who had a misunderstanding.'
choices.outcome_text: Tells us nothing specific. We're already bored.

choices.label: B. 'The day Aman accused me of stealing his pen, I knew our friendship was over before lunch.'
choices.learning_concept: Specific names + consequence + tension = great hook.
choices.outcome_text: Tension, stakes, specifics. We HAVE to keep reading. That's a hook.

choices.label: C. 'Misunderstandings can happen anywhere, anytime, to anyone.'
choices.outcome_text: Sounds like a textbook. Specific story > general statement.

choices.label: D. 'Once upon a time...'
choices.outcome_text: Cliché. Even fairy tales avoid it now. Find a fresh entry.

rounds.situation: Strong stories have three parts: SETUP (who/where), CONFLICT (what goes wrong), RESOLUTION (what changes). Read this draft about a lost dog. Pick how to fix it.
rounds.coaching_moment: Without a structure, even good sentences feel pointless. Bones first, then flesh.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do almost all stories — from epics to tweets — have a 3-part shape?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon storyboard with three panels labeled setup, conflict, resolution, friendly fox holding pencil, educational illustration
rounds.draft_excerpt: A boy lost his dog. He was sad. He found it. The end.

choices.label: A. Just add more adjectives: 'A young boy lost his beloved dog. He was very sad. Eventually he found it. The lovely end.'
choices.outcome_text: Same dead bones, just dressed up. The skeleton is still missing meat.

choices.label: B. Expand each part: SETUP (who, where, what's at stake), CONFLICT (what makes the search hard), RESOLUTION (how does it change him).
choices.learning_concept: Strong structure carries even simple plots.
choices.outcome_text: YES. Now ask: who's the boy? What's special about THIS dog? What goes wrong on the search? How is he different at the end? Suddenly there's a story.

choices.label: C. Make it longer with random details (the colour of the sky, the food the boy ate).
choices.outcome_text: Random detail bloats. Every detail should serve the structure.

choices.label: D. Cut the conflict — make him find the dog faster.
choices.outcome_text: If you remove the conflict, you remove the story. Conflict is the engine.

rounds.round_title: Round 4 — Voice (the only thing that's truly yours)
rounds.situation: The same scene — kid catches first fish — written in 4 voices. Which one feels most distinctive and alive?
rounds.coaching_moment: Voice is what makes you different. Two writers can describe the same lake; only one description sounds like YOU.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What 3 words describe YOUR voice when you write?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon four different writers at typewriters with speech bubbles in different colors, expressing same idea differently, educational

input_field.label: Optional: write 1 line in YOUR voice about catching a fish.

choices.label: A. 'The boy felt happy when he caught the fish. It was a good day.'
choices.outcome_text: No voice. Could be anyone. Forgettable.

choices.label: B. 'I yelled so loud my dad dropped his beer. The fish flopped on the dock like it was protesting being caught.'
choices.outcome_text: ALIVE. Voice + specifics + a tiny joke. We hear a person, not a textbook.

choices.label: C. 'In conclusion, the act of catching a fish is one that can bring great joy to a young angler.'
choices.outcome_text: Reads like a school report. Drain the formality. Sound like a person.

choices.label: D. 'It was a fish. He caught it. Wow.'
choices.learning_concept: Sparse ≠ punchy when there's nothing there.
choices.outcome_text: Brevity is great. Empty brevity isn't. Where's the SPECIFIC detail?

rounds.situation: First drafts are almost always weak. The skill is REVISION — re-reading and cutting. Here's a paragraph. What's the BEST revision approach?
rounds.coaching_moment: Most students hate revision because they confuse 'editing' with 'failure'. Real writers know revision IS the writing.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What's the difference between PROOFREADING and REVISING?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon writer with red pen marking up draft, friendly mascot Mento crossing out words, educational illustration
rounds.draft_excerpt: It was a really really hot day. The sun was very very bright. Many people were going about their day. One of them was a girl named Riya. She was walking. She was thinking about a lot of stuff. Her thoughts were quite confusing. She felt overwhelmed.

choices.label: A. Just fix typos. Don't change the words.
choices.outcome_text: That's proofreading, not revision. The structure is still flabby.

choices.label: B. Cut 'really really', 'very very', and 'a lot of stuff'. Replace with ONE specific image. Combine sentences.
choices.outcome_text: Now: 'The sun pressed down. Riya walked, replaying her mother's morning words.' Half the words. Twice the impact.

choices.label: C. Make it LONGER — add more description.
choices.outcome_text: Bad drafts get worse with more words. They need a sharper knife, not more clay.

choices.label: D. Throw it out and start over.
choices.learning_concept: Sometimes a sledgehammer is needed — but cutting is usually enough.
choices.outcome_text: Sometimes valid! But mostly drafts have something worth saving — find the gold, cut the rest.

rounds.situation: You've written your best piece. A trusted reader says: 'The ending feels rushed.' How do you respond?
rounds.coaching_moment: How writers RECEIVE feedback predicts whether they'll grow. Don't defend — listen.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why is the urge to defend our writing usually wrong?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon writer listening to friend's feedback with open notebook, both smiling, warm educational illustration

choices.label: A. 'No, the ending is fine — you didn't read it carefully.'
choices.outcome_text: Now they won't give you honest feedback again. You've trained them to lie.

choices.label: B. 'Tell me more. Where does it start to feel rushed? What did you want to know that wasn't there?'
choices.outcome_text: Now you have actionable info. The feedback is gold once you ask follow-ups.

choices.label: C. Smile and ignore it.
choices.outcome_text: Useless. You traded growth for ego.

choices.label: D. Rewrite the entire ending immediately based on their guess.
choices.outcome_text: Listening ≠ obeying. You're still the author. Process the feedback, then decide.

rounds.situation: Final piece for your portfolio: a 1-paragraph personal essay starting with 'I never expected ___'. Pick your APPROACH (not the words).
rounds.coaching_moment: Personal essays work when they trade BIG general claims for ONE small specific moment.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why does 'one small story' often feel more powerful than 'one big lesson'?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon writer writing personal memoir with single magical moment glowing on page, warm and cozy

input_field.label: Your personal essay starting with 'I never expected ___'

choices.label: A. Big philosophical statement: 'I never expected life to be so complex...'
choices.outcome_text: Sounds wise; reads forgettable. Trade abstraction for a moment.

choices.label: B. ONE specific moment: 'I never expected to cry the day my old phone broke — but I did, on the bus, like a fool.'
choices.learning_concept: Personal essays earn power through specific moments.
choices.outcome_text: Real. Specific. Vulnerable. Now you have a piece worth reading.

choices.label: C. Generic story everyone has: 'I never expected my first day of school to be so hard.'
choices.outcome_text: Everyone's written this. What's the version only YOU could write?

choices.label: D. Multiple stories at once: 'I never expected my dog, my school, my parents...'
choices.outcome_text: Pick ONE. Specific beats sprawling.

rounds.situation: You've written 7 pieces. Time to look back at YOUR writer's voice. Which pillar do you want to grow most next?
rounds.coaching_moment: The greatest writers know which muscle of theirs is weakest — and train it.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Which part of writing do you most enjoy? Which scares you?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon writer surrounded by stacked finished pieces, looking thoughtfully at notebook, mascot fox cheering

choices.label: A. Clarity — be more specific, cut the fog.
choices.outcome_text: Solid pick. Clarity is the skill that pays off in EVERY kind of writing.

choices.label: B. Structure — give my pieces real bones.
choices.outcome_text: Good. Structure is invisible when it works and obvious when it doesn't.

choices.label: C. Voice — sound more like ME, less like a textbook.
choices.outcome_text: Excellent. Voice is the slowest to grow — but the most lasting.

choices.label: D. Revision — actually rewrite instead of submitting first drafts.
choices.outcome_text: Great pick. Most amateur writers never revise. The pros do little else.

achievements.title: Strong Hook
achievements.criteria: Pick the strongest hook in Round 2.

glossary_terms.definition: The opening line/paragraph that grabs the reader.
The distinct way a writer sounds — tone, rhythm, word choice.
Use specific scenes/sensory details instead of telling readers what to feel.
Rewriting parts of a draft for clarity, structure, or voice — not just typos.
Setup → conflict → resolution, the bones of most stories.
Concrete, sensory detail. The opposite of vague.

endings.title: Writer in the Making
endings.message: You finished with strong voice AND strong clarity. Keep writing — your portfolio is the proof.

endings.title: Promising Voice
endings.message: Good run. Pick the pillar you scored lowest on and train it.

endings.title: First Drafts
endings.message: First drafts always feel rough. Write 5 more pieces and watch yourself grow.

checkpoints.prompt: Which of your pieces so far has the strongest bones?
When was the last time you got writing feedback? How did you handle it?

reflection_prompt: Which lever, if you'd moved it earlier, would have changed your outcome the most?
